questions.q: Who decides how much foreign aid the U.S. gives?
questions.brief: Congress sets nearly every aid account's funding each year in the State, Foreign Operations appropriations bill (food aid in the Agriculture bill, some military aid in Defense), under standing laws such as the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961; executive agencies then carry the programs out. Offices and committees, not people. Give no dollar figures from the CRS report, which is dated 2022. USAID stopped implementing foreign aid on July 1, 2025, and some of its work moved to the State Department: never name USAID as an agency that runs aid now (the past tense is fine).

questions.brief: Immediate relief after disasters and conflict against long-term work on health, growth, governance and education; examples of each. No dollar figures from the CRS report, which is dated 2022.

questions.q: What is the difference between bilateral and multilateral aid?
questions.brief: Aid the U.S. gives and runs itself for a country or region, against U.S. money pooled with other donors through international organizations and the multilateral development banks; the trade-off in control. Not the same as U.S. dues to the United Nations. No dollar figures from the CRS report, which is dated 2022. USAID stopped implementing foreign aid on July 1, 2025, and some of its work moved to the State Department: never name USAID as an agency that runs aid now (the past tense is fine).

questions.q: What is the difference between USAID and the State Department?
questions.brief: USAID was the lead development and humanitarian agency, set up in 1961 and reporting to the Secretary of State; the State Department runs diplomacy and supervises foreign aid. Then what changed in 2025: as of July 1, 2025, USAID stopped implementing foreign aid and some of its work moved to State. The offices, not the people holding them; plain dates and facts, no judgement.

questions.q: Who receives the most U.S. foreign aid?
questions.searched: who receives the most us foreign aid
questions.brief: The largest country recipients in fiscal 2025 with their amounts, and the share of that year's aid that went to global and regional programs rather than one country. Then, briefly, the largest so far in fiscal 2026, saying the year is only partly reported. Never say why a country got more.
